questions.q: Meena says: 'Shrines of religions that began outside India, such as Islam and Christianity, are visited only by followers of that religion, and only for everyday prayer.' Test her claim using the chapter. Which part is right and which is wrong?
questions.a: Her claim is partly right. Right: people do visit or gather in these places for prayer and worship. Wrong: followers of other faiths also visit them, for example the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer and the Velankanni Church; and people also go on pilgrimages to these shrines on special occasions, not only for everyday prayer.
s: Right part: these places are visited for prayer and worship
Wrong part: followers of other faiths also visit, with an example (Dargah Sharif of Ajmer or Velankanni Church)
Wrong part: people also make pilgrimages to them on special occasions, so the verdict is 'partly right'

questions.q:
A gurdwara committee in Delhi is organising a bus pilgrimage to the three Sikh takhts that the chapter names. 240 pilgrims have registered. Each bus seats 45 pilgrims. The trip costs Rs 3,600 per pilgrim, and the committee had promised to pay 25% of this cost for every pilgrim from its own fund.
(a) Name the three takhts the chapter gives, with the place of each.
(b) How many buses must the committee hire?
(c) How much money would the 25% promise need in all?
(d) The committee's fund has only Rs 2,00,000. Can it keep its promise? If not, find the largest whole-number percentage it can pay for all 240 pilgrims, and show your check.
questions.a: (a) Takht Sri Patna Sahib (Patna), the Akal Takht (part of the Golden Temple at Amritsar) and Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib (Anandpur). (b) 240 / 45 = 5.33, so 6 buses are needed (5 buses would seat only 225). (c) Total cost = 240 x 3,600 = Rs 8,64,000; 25% of it = Rs 2,16,000. (d) No: Rs 2,16,000 is more than Rs 2,00,000. 23% of Rs 8,64,000 = Rs 1,98,720, which fits, while 24% = Rs 2,07,360, which does not; so the largest whole-number share it can pay is 23%.
s: (a) Takht Sri Patna Sahib (Patna), Akal Takht (Amritsar), Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib (Anandpur)
(d) Cannot keep 25%; 23% = Rs 1,98,720 fits but 24% = Rs 2,07,360 does not, so 23%

questions.q:
In a class debate, Rohan argues: 'A sacred place is just a building where people pray.' Using the chapter, write a reply in five parts.
(a) Give the chapter's meaning of sacredness.
(b) Show that something other than a building can be sacred.
(c) Using one Buddhist and one Sikh example, show what makes such places sacred.
(d) Using one example, show that a sacred place can draw people of more than one faith.
(e) Give your judgement on Rohan's argument.
questions.a: (a) Sacredness is finding something of deep religious or spiritual significance, worthy of respect and reverence, holy or divine. (b) It can be a special kind of journey (a pilgrimage), the route it takes, or even the land covered, not only a building. (c) Buddhist sites are places the Buddha visited or where his relics are kept, such as Bodh Gaya where he attained enlightenment; Sikh takhts such as the Akal Takht are sacred because they are associated with important Sikh Gurus. So sacredness comes from links with great figures, not from the building alone. (d) Followers of other faiths also visit the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer or the Velankanni Church. (e) Rohan's argument is too narrow: a place is sacred because of what it means to people, and journeys, routes and land can be sacred too.
s: (a) Meaning: something of deep religious or spiritual significance, worthy of respect and reverence
(b) A journey (pilgrimage), its route or the land itself can be sacred
(c) Buddhist example linked to the Buddha and Sikh example linked to the Gurus
(d) A shrine visited by other faiths, e.g. Dargah Sharif of Ajmer or Velankanni Church
(e) Judgement: the argument is too narrow, with a reason

questions.q:

questions.q:
Girnar in Gujarat and Sabarimala in Kerala are both hill shrines.
(a) Why is a hill like Girnar sacred in the Jain tradition?
(b) What does the difficult trek to Sabarimala symbolise?
(c) State one difference in what makes the two places sacred.
questions.a: (a) Jain tirthas are places where the Tirthankaras attained liberation or where important events of their lives took place; hills they visited or meditated on are sacred. (b) The difficult trek symbolises the difficulties of the inner path. (c) Girnar is sacred because of its link with the Tirthankaras, the great figures of Jainism, while Sabarimala is a temple of the deity Ayyappa whose hard approach itself carries a meaning about the inner journey.
s: (a) Linked with the Tirthankaras: liberation or events of their lives
(b) The difficulties of the inner path
(c) Difference: Girnar's link with the Tirthankaras versus Sabarimala's deity Ayyappa and its symbolic trek

questions.a: (a) The wari goes to the Vithoba temple at Pandharpur in Maharashtra; Sabarimala is the temple of Ayyappa in Kerala. (b) The wari is an 800-year-old tradition in which pilgrims walk for 21 days; Sabarimala draws over ten million devotees every year. (c) In the wari pilgrims walk in large groups every year; Sabarimala was traditionally reached by an immensely difficult trek through hills and forests. (d) Both are physical journeys that are also inner journeys: the hardship of the walk stands for the difficulty of the inner path.
s: (a) Vithoba at Pandharpur (Maharashtra) and Ayyappa at Sabarimala (Kerala)
(b) Wari: 800 years old or 21 days; Sabarimala: over ten million a year
(c) Wari: walking in large groups annually; Sabarimala: difficult trek through hills and forests
(d) Shared idea: both a physical and an inner journey

questions.q:
Nehru wrote in 1961 that the 'feeling of one country and one culture' drew pilgrims from Badrinath, Kedarnath and Amarnath to Kanyakumari and back. Dharampal met about twelve pilgrims from two villages north of Lucknow returning from a three-month pilgrimage up to Rameswaram, carrying atta, ghee and sugar, and hurrying on to Haridwar.
(a) Which two ends of the country did this group's journey link?
(b) What do the length of the trip and the food they carried tell us about the pilgrimage?
(c) How does this one group's journey support Nehru's idea?
(d) State one limit of using a single group of about twelve people as proof of Nehru's idea.
(e) Give your judgement: how far does Dharampal's account support Nehru's statement?
questions.a: (a) The far south (Rameswaram) and the north (Haridwar, via their home near Lucknow). (b) A three-month trip with their own food shows it was a long, planned journey of effort and discipline, not a short outing. (c) Ordinary villagers from the north travelled to the far southern tip and on to a northern tirtha, so pilgrims really did move north to south and back, as Nehru said. (d) One group shows that such journeys happened, but not why all pilgrims travelled or that they felt 'one country and one culture'; that feeling is Nehru's interpretation. (e) The account supports the movement Nehru describes well, but supports the feeling behind it only partly; it is good evidence of the practice, weaker evidence of the motive.
s: (a) Rameswaram in the far south and Haridwar in the north
(b) Three months and own food: a long, disciplined journey of effort
(c) Villagers moved north to south and back, as Nehru says
(d) Limit: one small group cannot prove the motive or the feeling of all pilgrims
(e) Judgement: strong for the practice, partial for the feeling, with a reason

Read the passage and answer the questions.
A Class 7 group visits the Belur temple in Karnataka. On a wall they see a carving in which Vishnu, in the form of his boar avatar, crushes a demon and saves a goddess who sits on his elbow. A week later the group visits the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu, where a Toda guide points to a mountain peak, a patch of Shola forest and a wetland, and says his people hold all three sacred.
(a) In what form is Vishnu shown in the Belur carving?
(b) Which goddess does he save, and what does her name stand for?
(c) Name two of the places the Toda guide showed that his people hold sacred.
(d) Using the chapter, state the one idea that links the Belur carving and the Toda guide's places.
questions.a: (a) His boar avatar. (b) Bhudevi, who is Mother Earth. (c) Any two of the mountain peak, the Shola forest and the wetland. (d) Nature, and ultimately the whole Earth, is sacred, because a divine presence is perceived in all of Nature.
s: (a) The boar avatar
(b) Bhudevi, Mother Earth
(c) Any two of the peak, the Shola forest, the wetland
(d) Nature and the whole Earth are sacred: a divine presence in all of Nature

questions.q:
The chapter gives three examples of Nature held sacred: the Dongria Khond of Odisha, the Government of Sikkim, and the Todas of the Nilgiris.
(a) Dongria Khond: what is sacred, and what rule follows from it?
(b) Sikkim: what was identified, and for what purpose?
(c) Todas: what do they hold sacred, and how do plants enter their life?
(d) The Dongria Khond's rule about trees is a religious rule. Explain how it also helps to protect the hill's forest.
(e) What single idea do the three examples together show?
questions.a: (a) The Niyam Dongar hill, the abode of Niyam Raja; cutting trees there is prohibited. (b) Sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs were identified so that they could be protected against all forms of damage. (c) Many mountain peaks linked with their gods, plants, Shola forests, wetlands, stones and individual trees; plants often become part of their rituals. (d) Because cutting trees is forbidden as disrespect to Niyam Raja, the trees on the hill are left standing, so the forest is preserved; the chapter notes that seeing the landscape as sacred has helped to protect and preserve Nature. (e) That in many traditions elements of Nature are seen as sacred because a divine presence is perceived in Nature, and that this leads to their protection.
s: (a) Niyam Dongar hill, abode of Niyam Raja; no cutting of trees
(b) Mountains, caves, lakes, rocks, hot springs identified for protection from all damage
(c) Peaks, plants, Shola forests, wetlands, stones; plants used in rituals
(d) No trees are cut out of respect for the deity, so the forest survives: belief leads to protection
(e) Nature is held sacred, which leads to protecting it

questions.q: Raju says: 'In the past, only pilgrims made long journeys across India, so the old routes carried nothing but religious ideas.' Using the chapter, point out two errors in his statement.
questions.a: Error 1: pilgrims were not the only long-distance travellers; merchants and traders travelled to exchange goods, and others travelled to discuss, debate and popularise their beliefs or to study under eminent teachers. Error 2: the routes did not carry only religious ideas; where the routes converged, goods, experiences, tales and ideas were shared, new ideas emerged and old ones were adapted, which became a major factor in the cultural integration of the Subcontinent.
s: Error 1: others also travelled, e.g. merchants for trade, debaters or students for learning

(a) Find the percentage of each network she has completed.
(b) Which network is she nearest to completing?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why completing the Shakti pitha network would be hardest to do without leaving present-day India.

(c) The chapter says the Shakti pithas cover the whole map of India, even parts of present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan, so finishing that network would need travel outside present-day India.
s: (a) 75%, 50% and about 39%
(b) The jyotirlingas
(c) Some Shakti pithas lie in present-day Bangladesh and Pakistan

questions.q:
Imagine the diary of a pilgrim who walked an old route across the Subcontinent for 120 days. She records whom she walked with: 48 days with a merchants' caravan, 30 days with students going to study under a famous teacher, 12 days with a group of debaters, and the remaining days with other pilgrims. She writes that she learnt a new song from the students and a new tale from the merchants.
(a) Taking the merchants, students and debaters as non-pilgrims for this question, on what percentage of her days did she walk with travellers who were not pilgrims?
(b) According to the chapter, why did merchants, students and debaters each travel?
(c) Which process described in the chapter do her new song and tale show?
(d) A historian says, 'Pilgrims alone made the Subcontinent culturally integrated.' Use the diary and the chapter to judge her claim.
questions.a: (a) 48 + 30 + 12 = 90 days; 90 / 120 = 75%. (b) Merchants and traders travelled to exchange goods; students travelled to learn and study from eminent teachers; debaters travelled to discuss, debate and popularise their beliefs. (c) Where routes converged, travellers shared goods, experiences and tales, which enriched everyone; new ideas emerged and old ones were adapted. (d) The claim goes too far. Pilgrims mattered, but on this route three-quarters of her days were spent with other kinds of travellers, and the chapter says integration came from the meeting and sharing of all these groups on converging routes, not from pilgrims alone.
s: (b) Merchants: trade; students: study under teachers; debaters: discuss, debate and popularise beliefs
(c) Sharing of experiences and tales on converging routes; new ideas emerged
(d) Judgement: claim goes too far, since 75% of her company were others and integration came from all groups meeting

questions.q:
A museum plans a hall called 'Sacred Geography of India' and proposes to show only photographs of temples. You are asked to advise it. Using the chapter, write a five-part note.
(a) Explain what the chapter means by sacred geography.
(b) Explain how the story of the Shakti pithas makes the land itself sacred.
(c) Describe what pilgrims experienced as they covered the land.
(d) Explain the part played by other travellers on the same routes.
(e) Recommend whether photographs of temples alone are enough, and suggest one more kind of exhibit, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Networks of sacred places such as the char dham, the 12 jyotirlingas and the 51 Shakti pithas crisscross India's length and breadth, so the land itself becomes sacred. (b) The Shakti pithas are where parts of the divine mother's body fell across the Subcontinent; the symbol is that the whole land becomes her body. (c) Pilgrims covered India's geography and met diverse languages, customs, clothing and foods, but also noticed commonalities. (d) Merchants, debaters and students used the same routes; the sharing of goods, ideas and tales led to the cultural integration of the Subcontinent. (e) Temple photographs alone are not enough, because sacred geography is about networks, routes and the land as a whole; a map showing the networks of tirthas and their routes would show this, for example.
s: (a) Networks crisscrossing India make the land itself sacred
(b) Shakti pithas: the whole land becomes the divine mother's body
(c) Pilgrims met diverse languages, customs, foods and noticed commonalities
(d) Other travellers on the same routes: exchange leading to cultural integration
(e) Recommendation: photographs alone are not enough, plus a reasoned extra exhibit such as a map of networks

(b) The pitcher holding the amrita

questions.q:
Read the legend of amrita manthana in the chapter and answer.
(a) Why was it unusual that the devas and asuras worked together to churn the cosmic ocean?
(b) Why did Vishnu take the form of Mohini and snatch the kumbha?
(c) How does the legend explain why the Kumbh Mela is held at four places and not at one?
questions.a: (a) They were traditional enemies, and for once they joined forces. (b) To prevent the asuras from getting the amrita, the nectar of immortality. (c) While the kumbha was being snatched, a few drops of amrita fell at four places, Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain, so all four became places for the Mela.
s: (a) They were traditional enemies who joined forces only this once
(b) To keep the amrita from the asuras
(c) Drops fell at four places, so the Mela is held at all four

questions.q:
A city planning team studies the Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj. The chapter says about 660 million people took part in the Kumbh Mela of 2025. For this question, suppose the Mela lasted 45 days and the visitors were spread evenly over them. Each bathing ghat can serve 500,000 bathers in a day.
(a) What is the average number of visitors per day?
(b) How many ghats would be needed on an average day? Round up to a whole ghat.
(c) Using the chapter, explain why Prayag is a special place for a holy dip.
(d) A planner says, 'We only need to plan for the average day.' Using the chapter, judge whether this is wise.
questions.a: (a) 660,000,000 / 45 = about 14,666,667 visitors a day (about 14.7 million). (b) 14,666,667 / 500,000 = about 29.3, so 30 ghats. (c) Prayag lies at the confluence of the Ganga, the Yamuna and the invisible Sarasvati, and it is one of the four places where drops of amrita fell in the legend. (d) It is not wise. The chapter says a dip during a prescribed period is considered most auspicious, so crowds will gather on those days far above the average; the plan must cover the peak days, not just the average.
s: (a) 660 million / 45 = about 14.7 million a day
(b) 14.7 million / 500,000 = about 29.3, so 30 ghats
(c) Confluence of Ganga, Yamuna, invisible Sarasvati; a place where amrita fell
(d) Not wise: the prescribed period draws peak crowds, so plan for peaks

questions.q: Your teacher asks you to show four different ways in which rivers are treated as sacred in India. Using the chapter, give each way with one example or detail from the text. (Do not count the Kumbh Mela legend as more than one way.)
questions.a: Any four, each with a detail: (1) Rivers have been worshipped since Vedic times: the nadistuti sukta of the Rigveda praises 19 major rivers. (2) Rituals involving water invoke the important rivers: a verse calls on the Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu and Kaveri to be present in the water. (3) Rivers are spoken of with respect in local languages, as 'Ganga ji' or 'Yamuna ji'. (4) Their sources, tributaries and the places they flow through are regarded as sacred and visited by pilgrims; or many rivers are regarded as devis; or a dip at the Kumbh Mela places during the prescribed period is most auspicious.
s: Way 1: one distinct way rivers are treated as sacred, with a supporting detail from the chapter
Way 2: a second distinct way, with a supporting detail from the chapter
Way 3: a third distinct way, with a supporting detail from the chapter
Way 4: a fourth distinct way, with a supporting detail from the chapter (the Kumbh Mela counts only once)

questions.q:
A heritage quiz asks: 'Which is the better evidence that river worship in India is both very old and still alive today: the nadistuti sukta or the Kumbh Mela?'
(a) State what the nadistuti sukta is and what it praises.
(b) What does it show about river worship?
(c) Give two facts from the chapter about the Kumbh Mela of today.
(d) What does the Kumbh Mela show about river worship?
(e) Give your answer to the quiz question, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) It is a hymn of the Rigveda in praise of rivers that invokes 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India. (b) It shows that river worship is very old, going back to Vedic times. (c) Any two: about 660 million people took part in 2025; UNESCO has listed it as an intangible heritage of the world; it is held at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain. (d) It shows that river worship is alive today on a huge scale. (e) Neither alone answers both parts: the sukta proves age and the Kumbh proves that it is alive, so the best evidence is the two together; full credit also goes to a reasoned choice of one source that admits it shows only one half (age or present life).
s: (a) Rigvedic hymn invoking 19 rivers
(b) Shows river worship is very old (Vedic times)
(c) Two facts: 660 million in 2025, UNESCO intangible heritage, four places
(d) Shows river worship is alive today on a vast scale
(e) Judgement with a reason: both together, or a reasoned choice of one that admits what it does not show

questions.q: What is the botanical name of the peepul tree, also called the bo tree or bodhi tree?
questions.a: Ficus religiosa

questions.q: According to the chapter, why are many tirthas and temples in India located on hilltops?
questions.a: Because of their height, mountains are seen as a symbolic gateway from earth to heaven.
o: Because of their height, mountains are seen as a symbolic gateway from earth to heaven.
Because hilltops were safe from the floods of nearby rivers.
Because the major trade routes of ancient India ran over hilltops.
Because hilltops were easy to reach before modern roads were built.

questions.q:
Read the statements about sacred trees, forests and routes.
I. The peepul tree is sacred to Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and Jainism.
II. In Khasi (Meghalaya), a sacred grove is called a khlaw kyntang.
III. The Uttarapatha went from Kaushambi through Ujjain to Paithan.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Pilgrimage routes and trade routes in India often overlapped.
Reason (R): Pilgrims needed various items on their journeys, which traders could provide.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The chapter gives regional names for sacred groves. What is a sacred grove called in
(a) Malayalam?
(b) Marathi?
questions.a: (a) Kavu. (b) Devarai.
s: (a) Kavu
(b) Devarai

questions.q: True or False: 'The tree in the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is the very tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment.' Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the tree at Bodh Gaya is often cited as a direct descendant of the original tree under which, according to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha attained enlightenment; it is not the original tree itself.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: it is cited as a direct descendant of the original tree, not the original

questions.q:
Answer briefly about sacred groves.
(a) Name two harmful activities from which communities decided to protect some natural forests.
(b) What did these communities see such forests as?
(c) Give one way in which sacred groves help Nature.
questions.a: (a) Any two of hunting, tree felling and mining. (b) As the abodes of deities. (c) They shelter great biodiversity of plants and animals, or they hold small water bodies and help in water conservation.
s: (a) Two of hunting, tree felling, mining
(b) Abodes of deities
(c) Shelter biodiversity or help water conservation

questions.q:
A shrine in Bastar, Chhattisgarh, celebrates Rama's passing through the area.
(a) What do many rural and tribal traditions across India claim about the heroes of the Mahabharata and the Ramayana?
(b) How are such claims often marked on the ground?
(c) Villagers in two distant states each say that Rama passed through their own region. A classmate says one of them must be wrong, so such legends are useless. Using the chapter, explain why these local claims still matter for the two epics.
questions.a: (a) That the heroes of these epics passed through their own locality. (b) Shrines are often built to mark such passages, like the Bastar shrine. (c) The chapter's point is not whether each claim is literally accurate: by linking the epic heroes to their own land, such legends allowed a wide diversity of communities in many regions to make the two epics their own, so the claims from many places together spread the epics across the land.
s: (a) The epic heroes passed through their locality
(b) Shrines mark the places they passed
(c) The legends let diverse communities in many regions make the epics their own, so they matter whether or not each is literal

questions.q:
A state wants to protect a sacred river that is being over-used. Two plans are proposed. Plan A gives the river the rights and responsibilities of a human being, with community elders as its voice. Plan B adds the river to an official list of sacred sites to be protected against all forms of damage.
(a) Which example in the chapter is Plan A modelled on? Describe what happened there.
(b) Which example in the chapter is Plan B modelled on?
(c) Give one strength of each plan, using the chapter.
(d) Recommend one plan, or a mix, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) The Maori of New Zealand and the Taranaki Maunga mountain: after many representations, a law granted the mountain the rights and responsibilities of a human being, and the community's elders speak for it. (b) The Government of Sikkim, which in the early 2000s identified sacred mountains, caves, lakes, rocks and hot springs to be protected against all forms of damage. (c) Plan A: the people who hold the river sacred speak for it, which ensures it is not exploited. Plan B: a government list gives clear protection from all damage across many sites. (d) A reasoned choice, for example a mix: list the river officially (Plan B) and let the elders who revere it speak for it (Plan A), since the chapter shows both community voice and official protection help to save sacred places.
s: (a) Maori and Taranaki Maunga: legal rights of a person, elders speak for it
(b) Sikkim's early-2000s list of protected sacred sites
(c) One strength of each plan from the chapter
(d) A justified recommendation

questions.q:
A survey at the ghat of a sacred river found 1,200 kg of plastic waste in 2020 and 1,800 kg in 2025, although daily worship went on there throughout. Rekha says, 'Calling a river sacred is enough to keep it clean.'
(a) By what percentage did the waste rise from 2020 to 2025?
(b) What does the chapter say about the state of many sacred places today, and why?
(c) How did the sacred status of groves once help protect Nature?
(d) Whose duty does the chapter say it is to protect our national heritage?
(e) Judge Rekha's claim using your answers.
questions.a: (a) (1,800 - 1,200) / 1,200 x 100 = 50% rise. (b) Many sacred places, such as rivers like the Yamuna, Mahanadi and Kaveri, are polluted owing to widespread neglect and a lack of concern; the old harmonious relationship is under great strain. (c) Communities protected sacred groves from hunting, tree felling and mining because they saw them as abodes of deities, so the groves came to shelter great biodiversity. (d) It is our duty, as citizens, to protect our national heritage, as our Constitution also reminds us. (e) Rekha is wrong: the river was called sacred yet its waste rose by 50%. Sacredness protected the groves only because people acted on it; belief must be matched by action and care.
s: (b) Sacred places are polluted through neglect and lack of concern
(c) Groves were protected from hunting, felling and mining as abodes of deities
(d) Our duty, as the Constitution reminds us
(e) Judgement: the claim is wrong; sacredness works only when people act
